problem: Fixed-base manipulation foundation models cannot move the base, and end-to-end mobile manipulation lacks large-scale data. Naively chaining a navigation module with a manipulation module causes compounding errors because the robot stops at docking points from which the target cannot be manipulated (the last-mile problem).
motivation: Generalizable mobile manipulation is needed for household assistance, but mobile-manipulation demonstrations are very expensive to collect. The observation is that a subtask becomes easy for a fixed-base policy if the arm can reach the task-relevant keypoint of the target with enough motion margin. This lets docking-point selection be posed as a zero-shot geometric optimization guided by VLM keypoints.
key_idea: Use a VLM to pick a target keypoint on the object (multi-view voted) and an arm keypoint on the manipulator, then optimize base pose and arm joints to make them touch under collision, smoothness and margin costs, so the robot docks where any fixed-base policy can succeed.
insight: Multi-view keypoint fusion is the most important design choice: removing voting drops OVMM Overall SR from 20.64 to 15.19, and a single view gives 17.61. The three cost terms each help, and the margin cost helps most on pick-and-place (w/o Margin 17.87). Naive conventional navigation (L3MVN) improves FindRec by about 6.65 points but Overall SR by only 0.48, showing that reaching the vicinity of the target is not enough for manipulation. The visual backbone for keypoint proposals (DINOv2 vs CLIP or ViT) matters little.
method: Scene scan and task planning: the robot scans the scene to build a 3D point cloud and a ConceptGraphs scene graph; an LLM (GPT-4o in real world) decomposes the instruction into subtasks, each with one target object.
Keypoint proposal: DINOv2 pixel features, SAM part masks, and clustering of depth-normalized features per mask give candidate actionable points, in the style of ReKep.

Keypoint selection: candidates are indexed and drawn on the image, and a VLM picks the one that fits the subtask. The arm keypoint (AK) comes from the wrist camera, or is the end-effector position if the gripper is empty. For dual-arm robots, a VLM binary classifier picks the arm.

Multi-view voting for the target keypoint (TK): the VLM chooses top-V points in each of m object-centric views. These are back-projected to 3D, and each scene point is voted for by the proposals within a distance τ. The argmax point becomes TK.

Keypoint-guided optimization: minimize ||TK − AK(θ_base, θ_arm)|| plus costs. The collision cost uses query points on the robot surface against the scene point cloud with margin ε0. The smoothness cost penalizes changes in base and IK joint angles. The margin cost keeps the arm radius near the midpoint of [r_min, r_max].

Solver and execution: Dual Annealing searches base pose and arm joints, with Pinocchio IK. An existing navigation method first moves the robot near the target to shrink the search space. The fixed-base policy (Home-Robot, OpenVLA, AnyGrasp, iDP3, RDT-1B) then executes at the docking point.

setting.backbone: VLM (GPT-4o for real-world planning) with DINOv2 + SAM keypoint proposals, Dual Annealing optimization, and a plugged-in fixed-base policy (Home-Robot, OpenVLA fine-tuned with LoRA, AnyGrasp, iDP3, RDT-1B fine-tuned)
setting.training_data: MoTo itself is training-free/zero-shot. The plugged-in manipulation policies are fine-tuned separately: OpenVLA on 20k OVMM heuristic-collected pick-and-place samples, and RDT-1B / iDP3 on 50 demos per task for 3 real kitchen tasks.
setting.observation: RGB-D from an exterior/head camera and wrist cameras, SLAM pose, and a scanned 3D point cloud and scene graph
setting.action_space: Base pose (3-DoF, 2-DoF base movement) and 6-DoF arm joint targets with gripper, solved by optimization and IK, then executed by the fixed-base manipulation policy
setting.simulator: Habitat (OVMM / Home-Robot benchmark) and real world
setting.privileged: None stated beyond a prior scan of the whole scene (assumes all relevant objects are observable)

numbers.extra: OpenVLA fine-tuned on 20k OVMM expert samples; MoTo itself zero-shot

numbers_note: Real-world results are given only in a figure (10 runs per task type), so there are no table numbers. The abstract claims +16.67% real-world SR over the SOTA. The OVMM split is called the 'validation set'.
results: On OVMM, MoTo raises Home-Robot (RL) Overall SR from 14.80 to 18.32 and OpenVLA w/ MoTo reaches 20.64, above UniTeam's 17.96 and OpenVLA w/ L3MVN's 16.09. In the real world it improves over conventional navigation with AnyGrasp, iDP3 and RDT-1B on all three long-horizon tasks (the abstract states +16.67% SR).
limitations: Needs a full prior scan and offline scene reconstruction, so it cannot handle dynamic or partially observable scenes.
Only produces docking points, with no whole-body control, so tasks such as door opening fail.
Failure modes include SLAM localization errors, Dual Annealing loops, and jerky base motion, plus sensitivity of fixed-base policies to changed viewpoints.
